clarifyingQuestions: Does capacity count pending only or pending plus in-progress?
Should failed work retry at the front or back of the queue?
Should a production extension reject duplicate task IDs? The base queue treats repeated values as separate work.
followUps: Add task IDs and reject duplicate pending or active IDs.
Add per-worker leases that expire if a worker dies.
followUpGuide: For duplicate rejection, keep a set of item IDs covering both pending and in-progress. Remove IDs only on complete or final failure.

For leases, store `(item, lease_deadline, generation)` per assignment and reclaim expired leases into pending or dead-letter them. Require the assignment generation on complete/fail so a late response from an expired worker cannot remove a newer assignment. Lease expiry permits retries while an old attempt may still be running.
For thread safety, use one lock around pending and in-progress maps. Queue operations are small and should remain atomic.
complexityAnalysis: - Single-threaded deque + dict (graded solution): enqueue, start, complete, and fail take amortized O(1) deque work and expected O(1) dictionary work. Stored queue state uses O(p + w) space for p pending jobs and w active workers. Retries can make p exceed max_pending, so account for retry growth when bounding total memory.
- `snapshot()` copies pending and in-progress state for isolation. Time: O(p + w). Space: O(p + w) for the returned copy.
- Thread-safe / condition-variable follow-up keeps the same asymptotic operations under one lock; total wall time depends on task cost and worker count.
solutionGuide: Use a `deque` for pending work and a dictionary for worker ownership.

Capacity checks pending length. Once a worker starts an item, pending space opens up. A retry returns already accepted work to the queue even when admission capacity is full. Use `is not None` when deciding whether to requeue: zero and other falsey payloads are valid work. `snapshot` copies both containers while sharing references to item payloads.
